questions.prompt: What does a patent protect?
options: A new invention or process
A brand name or logo
A song or poem
A fabric pattern
questions.explanation: A patent protects new inventions — these can be new products or new processes that solve a technical problem.
questions.verify: Section 2(1)(j) of the Patents Act, 1970 defines 'invention'.

questions.prompt: A patent in India is valid for 20 years from the date of filing.
questions.explanation: Correct! Under Indian law, a patent is granted for 20 years from the date the application was filed.
questions.verify: Section 53 of the Patents Act, 1970 (as amended 2005).

questions.prompt: Who grants patents in India?
options: The Indian Patent Office
The Supreme Court of India
The Reserve Bank of India
The local police station
questions.explanation: Patents are granted by the Indian Patent Office, headed by the Controller General of Patents, Designs and Trade Marks.
questions.verify: The Patent Office functions under the Controller General — ipindia.gov.in/patent-offices.htm

questions.prompt: You can patent a mathematical formula in India.
questions.explanation: No! Mathematical methods, scientific theories and abstract ideas cannot be patented in India.
questions.verify: Section 3(c) of the Patents Act, 1970 excludes mere discovery of a scientific principle or formulation of an abstract theory.

questions.prompt: Which of these could be patented in India?
options: A new type of water filter that removes bacteria using a special material
A recipe for making dal (lentil curry)
The discovery that the Earth orbits the Sun
A way of doing yoga
questions.explanation: A new water filter with a special technical mechanism can be patented because it is a novel product solving a technical problem. Recipes, discoveries and traditional practices cannot be patented.
questions.verify: Section 3 of the Patents Act, 1970 lists non-patentable inventions.

questions.story: Ravi, a young engineer from Pune, has invented a new type of solar-powered water purifier. It uses a special ceramic membrane he designed that can clean 200 litres of water per hour — much faster than existing models.
questions.prompt: What should Ravi do to protect his invention?
options: File a patent application with the Indian Patent Office
Register a trademark for his name
Copyright the water purifier
Post about it on social media to prove he made it first
questions.explanation: Since Ravi created a new technical invention (a product), he should file a patent application. A patent will give him the exclusive right to make, sell and licence his water purifier for 20 years.
questions.verify: Section 48 of the Patents Act, 1970 – rights of patentees.

questions.prompt: What are the THREE requirements for an invention to be patentable in India?
options: Novelty, Inventive Step, Industrial Application
Creativity, Beauty, Usefulness
Popularity, Novelty, Low Cost
Originality, Trademark, Registration
questions.explanation: An invention must be Novel (new, not known before), involve an Inventive Step (not obvious to an expert), and have Industrial Application (can be made or used in industry).
questions.verify: Sections 2(1)(j), 2(1)(ja), 2(1)(ac) of the Patents Act, 1970.

questions.story: Dr. Meera, a scientist in Hyderabad, discovers a new plant species growing in the Western Ghats. She wants to patent the plant itself.
questions.prompt: Can Dr. Meera patent the plant she discovered?
options: No — plants and animals, and discoveries of living things found in nature, cannot be patented in India
Yes — any new discovery can be patented
Yes — but only if she gives it a unique name
No — only foreign companies can patent plants
questions.explanation: In India, plants, animals and biological processes for their production cannot be patented. Also, a mere 'discovery' of something existing in nature is not the same as an 'invention'.
questions.verify: Section 3(j) of the Patents Act, 1970 excludes plants and animals. Section 3(c) excludes mere discoveries.

questions.prompt: What does 'prior art' mean in patent law?
options: All existing knowledge and inventions before a patent application is filed
Art paintings made before 1900
The first draft of a patent application
A type of traditional Indian art
questions.explanation: 'Prior art' refers to all publicly available information (publications, products, demonstrations) that existed before the date of a patent filing. An invention must be new compared to prior art.
questions.verify: Section 2(1)(l) of the Patents Act, 1970 defines 'new invention' with reference to prior art.

questions.prompt: Sort these into 'Can Be Patented' and 'Cannot Be Patented' in India.

items.text: 🔋 A new type of battery
📐 A mathematical theorem
🚜 A new harvesting machine
🌱 A method of farming
💊 A new chemical compound for medicine
🪨 A discovery of a new mineral in nature

questions.explanation: New technical inventions (batteries, machines, chemical compounds) can be patented. Mathematical theorems, methods of agriculture, and mere discoveries of natural substances cannot.
questions.verify: Section 3 of the Patents Act, 1970 — list of non-patentable subject matter.

questions.story: You receive a case file about two tech companies in Bengaluru. Company A claims Company B stole their technology.
clues: 🔍 Clue 1: Company A spent 3 years developing a new algorithm that charges phone batteries 50% faster using a unique circuit design.
🔍 Clue 2: Company A filed a patent application for this technology 2 years ago, and the patent was granted 6 months ago.
🔍 Clue 3: Company B recently launched a phone charger that uses an almost identical circuit design, without any licence or agreement with Company A.
questions.prompt: What type of IP violation has most likely occurred?
options: Patent infringement
Trademark violation
Copyright infringement
Design theft
questions.explanation: Company A had a granted patent for their charging technology. Company B copied the patented circuit design without permission, which is patent infringement. Company A can file a case in court and seek damages.
questions.verify: Section 104 of the Patents Act, 1970 deals with patent infringement suits.

questions.story: An anonymous tip leads you to investigate a pharmaceutical company in Mumbai.
clues: 🔍 Clue 1: A small Indian pharma company developed a life-saving drug after 10 years of research and got a patent for it.
🔍 Clue 2: The drug costs ₹50,000 per month. Millions of patients cannot afford it.
🔍 Clue 3: The Indian government is considering issuing a 'compulsory licence' so other companies can manufacture a cheaper version.
questions.prompt: What is a 'compulsory licence' in patent law?
options: Government permission for others to make a patented product without the patent holder's consent, usually for public health reasons
A licence to drive a company vehicle
Permission to copy any patent freely
A licence given automatically to all companies
questions.explanation: A compulsory licence allows the government to permit other manufacturers to produce a patented product without the patent owner's agreement, typically when the product is not available at an affordable price or for public health emergencies. India used this provision in 2012 for the cancer drug Nexavar.
questions.verify: Section 84 of the Patents Act, 1970 deals with compulsory licences. India's first compulsory licence was granted in 2012 (Natco vs Bayer for Sorafenib Tosylate).

questions.prompt: Anita invents a new water-saving irrigation device. She publishes a paper about it in a science journal BEFORE filing a patent application. What happens?
options: Her invention may lose novelty because it was publicly disclosed before filing — she should have filed first
Nothing — publishing helps get a patent faster
The journal automatically files the patent for her
She can still patent it anytime within 10 years
questions.explanation: In India, if an invention is publicly disclosed (published, presented, sold) before filing a patent application, it may lose the 'novelty' requirement and become unpatentable. Always file first, publish later!
questions.verify: Section 25(1)(b) and Section 64(1)(e) of the Patents Act, 1970 — prior publication can be grounds for refusal or revocation.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a 'product patent' and a 'process patent'?
options: A product patent protects the final product itself; a process patent protects the method used to make it
They are the same thing with different names
A product patent is for food items; a process patent is for machines
A product patent lasts longer than a process patent
questions.explanation: A product patent protects the actual product (e.g., a new drug molecule). A process patent protects only the method of making it — others can make the same product using a different process. India introduced product patents for all fields in 2005.
questions.verify: The Patents (Amendment) Act, 2005 introduced product patents for all fields including pharmaceuticals and food, as required by the TRIPS Agreement.

questions.prompt: A farmer in Punjab has been using a traditional method of pest control passed down for generations. Can a company patent this traditional method?
options: No — traditional knowledge that is already publicly known cannot be patented because it lacks novelty
Yes — whoever files first gets the patent
Yes — but only if the company improves the method slightly
No — only the government can patent traditional knowledge
questions.explanation: Traditional knowledge already in the public domain cannot be patented because it is not 'novel'. India created the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) to document traditional knowledge and prevent others from wrongly patenting it.
questions.verify: Section 3(p) of the Patents Act, 1970 (as amended 2005) excludes inventions that are traditional knowledge. The TKDL has prevented over 200 patent applications worldwide.

questions.prompt: What is a trademark?
options: A sign (like a name, logo or symbol) that identifies and distinguishes one brand's products from others
A type of tax on imported goods
A special stamp on exported products
A government permit to start a business
questions.explanation: A trademark is any sign that can distinguish the goods or services of one business from those of others. Think of brand names like 'Amul' or logos like the Tata 'T'!
questions.verify: Section 2(1)(zb) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 defines 'trade mark'.

questions.prompt: The ™ symbol means a trademark is officially registered with the government.
questions.explanation: The ™ symbol means someone is USING a mark as a trademark, but it may not be registered. The ® symbol means the trademark IS officially registered with the Trade Marks Registry.
questions.verify: Section 28 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 — rights conferred by registration. The ® symbol may only be used after registration.

questions.prompt: How long does a registered trademark last in India?
options: 10 years, renewable indefinitely for 10-year periods
20 years, then it expires
5 years, non-renewable
100 years
questions.explanation: A registered trademark in India is valid for 10 years from the date of registration. It can be renewed every 10 years, forever, as long as the owner keeps using it and pays the renewal fee.
questions.verify: Section 25 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 — duration and renewal of registration.

questions.prompt: A tagline or slogan (like 'Taste the Thunder') can be registered as a trademark in India.
questions.explanation: Yes! Slogans, taglines and catch phrases can be registered as trademarks if they are distinctive and identify a particular brand's goods or services.
questions.verify: Section 2(1)(zb) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 includes any word or combination of words in the definition of a mark.

questions.prompt: Why are trademarks important for consumers (buyers)?
options: They help consumers identify genuine products and avoid fakes
They make products more expensive
They are only important for the company, not the consumer
They guarantee the product will never break
questions.explanation: Trademarks help consumers quickly recognise which company made a product. Without trademarks, it would be easy to sell fake or low-quality goods by pretending they are from a trusted brand.
questions.verify: One of the key objectives of trademark law is consumer protection — preventing confusion and deception in the marketplace.

questions.story: Geeta starts a bakery in Jaipur called 'Royal Bakes' with a crown logo. After her bakery becomes popular, she discovers another bakery in the same city has opened as 'Royale Bakes' with a very similar crown logo.
questions.prompt: What should Geeta do?
options: Register her trademark (if not already done) and send a legal notice to the other bakery for trademark infringement
Ignore it — names are free for everyone to use
Change her own bakery's name to avoid conflict
Report it to the food safety department
questions.explanation: The other bakery is using a confusingly similar name and logo, which could mislead customers. Geeta should register her trademark and take legal action for infringement and passing off.
questions.verify: Section 29 (infringement) and Section 27 (no action for passing off prevented) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between ™ and ® symbols?
options: ™ means the mark is being used as a trademark (may not be registered); ® means it is officially registered
™ is for products and ® is for services
™ is old and ® is new — they mean the same thing
™ is used in India and ® is used internationally
questions.explanation: Anyone can use the ™ symbol to indicate they are using a sign as a trademark. But the ® symbol can ONLY be used after the trademark is officially registered with the Trade Marks Registry. Using ® falsely is a punishable offence!
questions.verify: Section 107 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 — penalty for falsely representing a trade mark as registered.

questions.story: Arjun finds a street market in Delhi selling sports shoes with a logo that looks almost exactly like a famous international sports brand's logo. The shoes are much cheaper than the original.
questions.prompt: What type of IP problem is this?
options: Counterfeiting — making and selling fake goods with a copied trademark
Fair competition — anyone can make similar products
Copyright infringement — copying the shoe design
Patent violation — copying the shoe technology
questions.explanation: This is counterfeiting — manufacturing or selling goods with a fake or copied trademark to mislead buyers into thinking they are buying genuine branded products. Counterfeiting is a criminal offence in India.
questions.verify: Section 103 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 — penalty for applying false trade marks.

questions.prompt: Sort these into 'Can Be a Trademark' and 'Cannot Be a Trademark' in India.

items.text: 🏷️ A unique brand name (e.g., 'Amul')
🎵 A distinctive jingle or sound
📝 A common dictionary word used in its ordinary meaning (e.g., 'Sweet' for a sweet shop)
🎨 A unique combination of colours for a brand
🗺️ The name of a geographical location used to describe where goods come from (e.g., 'Darjeeling' for any tea)
⭐ A distinctive logo or symbol

questions.explanation: Distinctive names, logos, sounds, and colour combinations can be trademarks. But common descriptive words and geographical names used generically usually cannot be registered as they need to be available for everyone to use.
questions.verify: Sections 9 and 11 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 list grounds for refusal of registration.

questions.story: A popular restaurant chain 'Desi Dhaba' discovers that a new restaurant 500 km away has opened as 'Desi Dhaba' with the same style of signage and menu layout.
questions.prompt: Does the original 'Desi Dhaba' have a case, even if the new restaurant is in a different city?
options: Yes — if 'Desi Dhaba' is a registered trademark, it is protected across all of India, regardless of distance
No — trademarks only apply within the same city
No — 'Desi Dhaba' is too generic to protect
Yes — but only if both restaurants serve the same food
questions.explanation: A registered trademark provides protection throughout India. Even if the infringing restaurant is in a different city, the trademark owner can take action. However, the name must be distinctive enough to qualify for trademark registration.
questions.verify: Section 28 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 — registration gives exclusive rights throughout India.

questions.story: You are called to investigate a major counterfeiting operation in a metropolitan city.
clues: 🔍 Clue 1: Customs officials at a port seized a container of electronic accessories (chargers, cables, earphones) with logos and packaging identical to a well-known brand.
🔍 Clue 2: Laboratory testing showed the products were of much lower quality and could even be unsafe — some chargers had no safety certification.
🔍 Clue 3: The genuine brand is registered as a 'Well-Known Trademark' in India and has never authorised this manufacturer.
questions.prompt: Why is counterfeiting especially dangerous in this case?
options: The fake products use a trusted brand's trademark to sell unsafe goods, putting consumers at physical risk
It makes the original products cheaper
It helps consumers get affordable alternatives
It only affects the brand's profits, not consumers
questions.explanation: Counterfeiting is not just about money — fake electronic products using a trusted trademark can be genuinely dangerous. Consumers trust the brand name and expect safety standards. Counterfeit chargers have caused fires and electric shocks. This is why trademark protection matters for consumer safety.
questions.verify: Section 29 and 103 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999. The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) requires safety certification for electronic goods.

questions.story: A famous Indian snack brand suspects their trademark is being misused online.
clues: 🔍 Clue 1: Someone registered a website domain name that is nearly identical to the snack brand's name, with just one letter different.
🔍 Clue 2: The website sells a completely different product (clothing) but uses the snack brand's colours and font style.
🔍 Clue 3: Many customers are confused and have sent complaints to the real snack brand about orders they never placed.
questions.prompt: What IP issue is happening here?
options: Cybersquatting and trademark dilution — using a famous mark's reputation to mislead online consumers
Copyright infringement of the website design
Patent infringement of the brand's recipe
Design copying of the brand's packaging
questions.explanation: This is cybersquatting (registering a domain similar to a famous trademark) and trademark dilution (weakening a famous mark's distinctiveness). In India, domain disputes can be resolved through the .IN Domain Dispute Resolution Policy (INDRP) or court action.
questions.verify: Section 29(4) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 deals with use of a mark similar to a well-known trademark. INDRP (IN Domain Dispute Resolution Policy) handles domain disputes.

questions.prompt: A company makes high-quality pickles and wants to use the word 'Aachar' (Hindi for pickle) as their trademark. Will this likely be approved?
options: Unlikely — 'Aachar' directly describes the product (pickle) and lacks distinctiveness for that product category
Yes — any word can be a trademark
Yes — Hindi words are always registrable
No — only English words can be trademarks in India
questions.explanation: Descriptive words that directly describe the product (like 'Aachar' for pickles or 'Cold' for ice cream) are usually refused registration because they lack distinctiveness. Other pickle companies also need to use the word 'Aachar'. However, a unique combination like 'Aachar Magic' might be distinctive enough.
questions.verify: Section 9(1)(b) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 — marks that consist exclusively of descriptive indications shall not be registered.

questions.prompt: What is 'trademark dilution'?
options: When the distinctiveness or reputation of a famous trademark is weakened by others using similar marks, even on different products
When a trademark is not renewed and expires
When a trademark is translated into another language
When two identical trademarks are registered in the same class
questions.explanation: Trademark dilution happens when a well-known mark's unique identity is weakened. For example, if someone starts a 'Tata Chai Stall' — even though Tata does not sell chai from stalls — it could dilute the TATA trademark's prestige and distinctiveness.
questions.verify: Section 29(4) of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 protects well-known marks against dilution.

questions.prompt: Priya creates a fan page on social media called 'We Love [Famous Brand]' using the brand's official logo as the page picture. Is this trademark infringement?
options: It could be — using someone's registered trademark (especially their logo) without permission, even on a fan page, can constitute infringement if it creates confusion
No — fan pages are always allowed
No — social media is outside trademark law
Yes — but only if she sells products on the page
questions.explanation: Using a registered trademark (especially the official logo) without authorisation can be infringement if it is likely to cause confusion or suggest an official connection. Even well-intentioned fan pages should be clearly marked as unofficial and ideally avoid using the official logo directly.
questions.verify: Section 29 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999 — use of a mark identical or similar to a registered trademark.

questions.prompt: What does copyright protect?
options: Original creative works like books, music, paintings, films and software
Brand names and logos
New inventions and machines
The shape of a product
questions.explanation: Copyright protects original literary, dramatic, musical, artistic works, cinematograph films, and sound recordings. If you write a story, compose a song, or paint a picture, copyright protects your creation!
questions.verify: Section 13 of the Copyright Act, 1957 lists works in which copyright subsists.

questions.prompt: In India, copyright for a book lasts for the author's lifetime plus 60 years.
questions.explanation: Correct! For literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works, copyright lasts for the author's lifetime plus 60 years after the year of the author's death.
questions.verify: Section 22 of the Copyright Act, 1957 — term of copyright in published literary, dramatic, musical and artistic works.

questions.prompt: Which of these is automatically protected by copyright the moment it is created?
options: A poem written in a notebook
A brand name for a shop
An idea for a new machine
The name of a character (just the name)
questions.explanation: A poem is an original literary work and gets copyright protection automatically the moment it is written down. Ideas, names and brand names are not protected by copyright. Remember — copyright protects the EXPRESSION of ideas, not the ideas themselves!
questions.verify: Section 13 of the Copyright Act, 1957. Copyright protects expression, not ideas.

questions.prompt: You must register your work with the Copyright Office to get copyright protection in India.
questions.explanation: No! Copyright protection is AUTOMATIC in India. You get it the moment you create an original work. Registration is optional but recommended because it serves as evidence of ownership in case of a dispute.
questions.verify: The Copyright Act, 1957 does not require registration for copyright to subsist. Section 45 allows voluntary registration.

questions.prompt: Aarav writes a beautiful poem. Who is the first owner of the copyright?
options: Aarav — the person who creates the work is usually the first owner
His school, because he is a student
The government of India
Nobody — poems cannot be copyrighted
questions.explanation: The author (creator) of a work is generally the first owner of copyright. If Aarav wrote the poem on his own (not as part of employment), he owns the copyright.
questions.verify: Section 17 of the Copyright Act, 1957 — first owner of copyright.

questions.story: Kavya writes a beautiful poem and shares it with her best friend Nisha. Without asking Kavya, Nisha copies the poem and submits it to a school magazine under her own name. The poem gets published.
questions.prompt: What IP wrong has Nisha committed?
options: Copyright infringement and violation of moral rights — she copied the poem without permission and claimed to be the author
No wrong — sharing means giving permission to use
Only a school rule violation, not a legal issue
Trademark infringement
questions.explanation: Nisha infringed Kavya's copyright by copying and publishing the poem without permission. She also violated Kavya's moral rights by not giving her credit (right of paternity) and by falsely claiming authorship. This is both morally wrong and legally actionable.
questions.verify: Section 51 (infringement) and Section 57 (moral rights — right of paternity and right of integrity) of the Copyright Act, 1957.

questions.prompt: What is 'fair dealing' (fair use) under Indian copyright law?
options: Limited use of copyrighted works allowed without the owner's permission for purposes like education, research, criticism, and news reporting
Buying a product at a fair price
Sharing copyrighted content on social media
Making exact copies for selling at a lower price
questions.explanation: Fair dealing allows limited use of copyrighted works without permission for specific purposes: private study, research, criticism, review, news reporting, and educational instruction. But it does not allow unlimited copying!
questions.verify: Section 52 of the Copyright Act, 1957 lists acts that are not infringement of copyright (fair dealing provisions).

questions.story: Rahul finds a popular movie on an illegal website and downloads it for free. He then shares the downloaded movie with 10 friends via a pen drive.
questions.prompt: Has Rahul violated copyright law?
options: Yes — downloading from illegal sources and distributing copies is copyright infringement (piracy)
No — downloading for personal use is always allowed
No — only the website owner is responsible, not the downloader
Yes — but only the sharing part, not the downloading
questions.explanation: Both downloading from an illegal source AND distributing copies (sharing) are copyright infringement. Movie piracy costs the Indian film industry thousands of crores every year and affects everyone from actors to technicians.
questions.verify: Section 51 of the Copyright Act, 1957 — acts that constitute infringement. Section 63 provides criminal penalties for piracy.

questions.prompt: Sort these into 'Fair Dealing (Allowed)' and 'Copyright Infringement (Not Allowed)' in India.

items.text: 📚 A student photocopying 2 pages from a book for study notes
🎬 Uploading a full movie to YouTube without permission
📰 A newspaper quoting a few lines from a speech for a news report
📀 Selling pirated copies of music CDs in a market
🎓 A teacher showing a short film clip in class for teaching
📖 Photocopying an entire textbook and selling copies to classmates

questions.explanation: Fair dealing allows limited copying for study, news, criticism and teaching. But copying entire works, uploading without permission, and selling pirated copies are all infringement.
questions.verify: Section 52 of the Copyright Act, 1957 — fair dealing exceptions. Section 51 — what constitutes infringement.

questions.prompt: Who generally owns the copyright in a Bollywood film?
options: The producer of the film
The lead actor
The director
The screenwriter
questions.explanation: Under Indian copyright law, the producer is the first owner of copyright in a cinematograph film (movie). However, the director, music composer, lyricist and other creators retain copyright in their individual contributions.
questions.verify: Section 17(b) of the Copyright Act, 1957 — for cinematograph films, the producer is the first owner.

questions.story: The Cyber Crime Unit receives a tip about a large-scale digital piracy operation.
clues: 🔍 Clue 1: A website is offering free downloads of hundreds of Bollywood and regional-language films, TV shows and music albums.
🔍 Clue 2: The website earns money through advertisements — it gets paid for every visitor who clicks on an ad.
🔍 Clue 3: None of the content on the website is uploaded with the permission of the copyright holders. The website operators are based in India.
questions.prompt: What crimes are the website operators committing?
options: Criminal copyright infringement — distributing copyrighted works without permission for commercial gain
Only a minor civil offence with no serious consequences
No crime — content on the internet is free for everyone
Only the uploaders are responsible, not the website owners
questions.explanation: Operating a piracy website is criminal copyright infringement under Indian law. The operators are distributing copyrighted works without permission and making money from it. This is punishable with imprisonment up to 3 years and fines. Indian courts have ordered the blocking of many such piracy websites.
questions.verify: Section 63 of the Copyright Act, 1957 — punishment for infringement (imprisonment up to 3 years, fine up to ₹2 lakh). Indian courts have issued 'John Doe' orders blocking piracy websites.

questions.story: A popular musician files a complaint about their songs being used without credit.
clues: 🔍 Clue 1: A composer created an original musical composition for an independent film. The producer paid the composer and the film was released.
🔍 Clue 2: The producer then used the same music in advertisements and a web series without informing the composer.
🔍 Clue 3: The advertisements and web series did not credit the composer at all. The composer's name was removed from the credits.
questions.prompt: What rights of the composer have been violated?
options: Both economic rights (using the music beyond the agreed scope) and moral rights (removing credit)
No rights — the producer paid for the music and owns it completely
Only moral rights — the producer can use the music however they want after paying
Only economic rights — credit is not a legal requirement
questions.explanation: The composer's economic rights were violated because the music was used beyond what was agreed (advertisements and web series were not part of the original deal). The moral right of paternity (right to be credited as the author) was also violated by removing the composer's name. Moral rights in India cannot be transferred even if economic rights are sold.
questions.verify: Section 57 of the Copyright Act, 1957 — author's special rights (moral rights) exist independently of copyright and remain with the author even after assignment of copyright.

questions.prompt: Sanya creates a beautiful digital painting and posts it on Instagram. A company downloads it and prints it on T-shirts to sell without her permission. The company says 'it was on the internet, so it's free.' Are they right?
options: No — posting something online does NOT give up copyright; the company committed infringement by using her artwork commercially without permission
Yes — anything posted publicly online is free to use
Partially — they can use it if they credit Sanya
It depends on how many T-shirts they sold
questions.explanation: Posting a work online does NOT mean giving up copyright. Sanya owns the copyright in her digital painting. The company using it commercially without her permission is copyright infringement, regardless of where they found it. Sanya can demand they stop and pay compensation.
questions.verify: Section 14 and Section 51 of the Copyright Act, 1957. Copyright applies to works published in any medium, including digital/online.

questions.prompt: How long does copyright last for a sound recording (song) in India?
options: 60 years from the year of publication
The performer's lifetime plus 60 years
20 years from recording
Forever
questions.explanation: Copyright in a sound recording (and cinematograph films) lasts for 60 years from the beginning of the calendar year following the year in which it was published. This is different from literary works, which last the author's lifetime plus 60 years.
questions.verify: Section 26 of the Copyright Act, 1957 — term of copyright in sound recordings.

questions.prompt: Can a student use a copyrighted image from the internet in their school project?
options: Generally yes — for private study and educational purposes, limited use is allowed under fair dealing, but they should give credit to the creator
No — all copyrighted images are completely off-limits
Yes — students are exempt from all copyright laws
Only if they pay the copyright owner first
questions.explanation: Fair dealing in India allows limited use of copyrighted works for private study, research, and education. A student using an image in a school project (not for commercial sale) is generally covered. However, they should always credit the source!
questions.verify: Section 52(1)(a) of the Copyright Act, 1957 — fair dealing for private or personal use, including research.

questions.prompt: What does a registered design protect?
options: The visual appearance of a product — its shape, pattern, or ornamentation
How a machine works inside
The brand name on a product
The story printed on a product's packaging
questions.explanation: A design registration protects the aesthetic (visual) features of an article — how it LOOKS, not how it works. This includes the shape, configuration, pattern, ornamentation, or composition of lines and colours.
questions.verify: Section 2(d) of the Designs Act, 2000 defines 'design'.

questions.prompt: A registered design in India is initially valid for 10 years from the date of registration.
questions.explanation: Correct! A registered design in India is initially protected for 10 years. After that, it can be extended for one more period of 5 years (total 15 years).
questions.verify: Section 11 of the Designs Act, 2000 — duration of registration.

questions.prompt: Which of these could be registered as a design?
options: The unique shape of a perfume bottle
The chemical formula of the perfume inside
The brand name 'Fragrance King' on the bottle
A TV advertisement for the perfume
questions.explanation: The unique shape of a perfume bottle is a visual feature that can be registered as a design. The chemical formula would be a patent matter, the brand name is a trademark, and the advertisement involves copyright.
questions.verify: Section 2(d) of the Designs Act, 2000 — design relates to features of shape, configuration, pattern or ornament applied to an article.

questions.prompt: The mechanical function of a product (how it works) can be protected by design registration.
questions.explanation: No! Design registration only protects how a product LOOKS, not how it works. If you want to protect how something works, you need a patent. A design is judged solely by the eye.
questions.verify: Section 2(d) of the Designs Act, 2000 — design features are 'applied to any article' and 'judged solely by the eye'.

questions.prompt: Meena makes beautiful clay pots with unique patterns carved into them. What type of IP should she use to protect the pattern?
options: Design registration — to protect the unique visual pattern on her pots
Patent — because she invented the pot
Trademark — because the pattern is her brand
Copyright — because clay pots are artistic works
questions.explanation: The unique decorative pattern applied to the pots is a 'design' in IP terms. Meena should register it as a design to prevent others from copying the pattern. Note: the pot itself is not a new invention (so no patent needed), and the pattern is not a brand identifier (so not a trademark).
questions.verify: Section 2(d) of the Designs Act, 2000 — 'pattern' and 'ornament' applied to an article are registrable as designs.

questions.story: Rajan, a potter in Khurja (famous for ceramics), creates a beautiful new vase shape that nobody has made before. He sells many vases at a craft fair. Two months later, he sees a factory mass-producing vases with the exact same shape.
questions.prompt: What should Rajan have done to protect his vase design?
options: Registered his new vase shape as a design with the Patent Office before selling it publicly
Applied for a trademark for the vase shape
Filed a copyright for the vase
Done nothing — pottery designs cannot be protected
questions.explanation: Rajan should have registered his unique vase shape as a design BEFORE making it public. Once a design is publicly disclosed (sold, exhibited), it may lose its 'novelty' and become harder to register. The lesson: register first, sell later!
questions.verify: Section 4 of the Designs Act, 2000 — a design must be 'new or original' and not 'previously published' to be registrable.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum total protection period for a registered design in India?
options: 15 years (initial 10 years + 5-year extension)
20 years
10 years (no extension possible)
25 years
questions.explanation: A registered design in India is initially valid for 10 years. The owner can apply for one extension of 5 years, giving a maximum total protection of 15 years.
questions.verify: Section 11(2) of the Designs Act, 2000 — copyright in design may be extended for a further period of 5 years.

questions.story: Fatima, a textile designer in Varanasi, creates a stunning new saree border pattern inspired by Mughal architecture. She wants to protect her pattern so that other weavers cannot copy it exactly.
questions.prompt: What should Fatima do?
options: Register the border pattern as a design — it protects the visual pattern applied to textiles
File a patent for the pattern — it is a new creation
Trademark the pattern — it identifies her brand
Do nothing — textile patterns cannot be protected in India
questions.explanation: Fatima's unique border pattern is a 'design' — a visual feature (pattern/ornament) applied to an article (saree). By registering it, she can prevent others from copying the exact pattern for up to 15 years. India's textile industry uses design registration extensively.
questions.verify: Section 2(d) of the Designs Act, 2000 — 'pattern' applied to any article by industrial process is registrable as a design.

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between a design and a patent?
options: A design protects the visual appearance of a product; a patent protects how a product works (its technical function)
There is no difference — they are the same thing
A design is for small products; a patent is for large machines
A design lasts longer than a patent
questions.explanation: The key difference: Design = how it LOOKS (aesthetic/visual features). Patent = how it WORKS (technical function/invention). A product can have both — for example, a uniquely shaped smartphone (design) that uses a new battery technology (patent).
questions.verify: Designs Act, 2000 vs Patents Act, 1970 — designs protect visual appeal, patents protect technical innovation.

questions.prompt: Sort these into 'Protected by Design Registration' and 'NOT Protected by Design Registration'.

items.text: ✏️ The unique shape of a pen
⚙️ The internal mechanism of a clock
🧶 A new embroidery pattern on a kurta
📖 The story written in a book
💎 The ornamental design of a piece of jewellery
🏷️ The brand name printed on a product

questions.explanation: Design registration protects visual features — shapes, patterns, and ornamentation. It does NOT protect how things work (patents), stories/text (copyright), or brand names (trademarks).
questions.verify: Section 2(d) of the Designs Act, 2000 — design means features of shape, configuration, pattern, ornament or composition of lines or colours.

questions.story: A famous Indian toy company files a complaint about their product designs being copied.
clues: 🔍 Clue 1: The company spent 2 years designing a line of educational toys with unique animal shapes and bright colour patterns. They registered the designs.
🔍 Clue 2: A competitor started selling almost identical toys through online marketplaces at half the price.
🔍 Clue 3: The competitor's toys have the same shapes and colour patterns but are made with cheaper, low-quality materials.
questions.prompt: What can the original toy company do?
options: File a design infringement case — the competitor has copied their registered designs without permission
Nothing — toys are too simple to be protected
Only complain to the online marketplace
File a patent infringement case
questions.explanation: Since the company registered their toy designs, they have exclusive rights to the visual appearance. The competitor copying the shapes and patterns without permission is design infringement. The company can seek a court injunction to stop the competitor and claim damages.
questions.verify: Section 22 of the Designs Act, 2000 — piracy of registered design. The registered proprietor can sue for infringement.

questions.story: A mobile phone manufacturer suspects their latest phone design is being copied.
clues: 🔍 Clue 1: The company launched a phone with a distinctive hexagonal camera module and curved edges — a design registered with the Indian Patent Office.
🔍 Clue 2: Three months later, a new brand released a phone that looks remarkably similar with the same hexagonal camera layout and curved edges.
🔍 Clue 3: However, the new brand's phone uses completely different internal hardware and software.
questions.prompt: Is this still design infringement even though the internal technology is different?
options: Yes — design infringement is about visual similarity, regardless of the internal technology
No — different technology means no infringement
Only if both phones have the same price
Only if customers complain about confusion
questions.explanation: Design protection is about visual appearance, not internal technology. If the external design (shape, pattern, ornamentation) of the competitor's phone is substantially similar to the registered design, it is infringement — even if the technology inside is completely different.
questions.verify: Section 2(d) and Section 22 of the Designs Act, 2000 — design is judged solely by the eye.

questions.prompt: Can the same product be protected by BOTH a design registration AND copyright?
options: Generally no — in India, if a design is registrable under the Designs Act and is applied to more than 50 articles, it cannot claim copyright protection
Yes — all products automatically get both
No — only one type of IP can protect any product
Yes — but only if you pay extra fees
questions.explanation: In India, there is an important overlap rule: if a design is registrable under the Designs Act and is reproduced more than 50 times by an industrial process, it loses copyright protection under the Copyright Act. This prevents 'double protection'. For unique handcrafted pieces (less than 50), copyright may still apply.
questions.verify: Section 15(2) of the Copyright Act, 1957 — copyright in any design capable of being registered under the Designs Act shall cease if the design has been applied to more than 50 articles.

questions.prompt: Vikram designs a chair that has a unique ergonomic shape. The shape serves BOTH an aesthetic purpose (looks beautiful) and a functional purpose (provides back support). Can the shape be registered as a design?
options: Only the aesthetic/visual aspects of the shape can be design-registered; the functional aspects would need a patent
Yes — the entire shape including its function is covered by design registration
No — if a shape has any function, it cannot be a design
Only if the chair is made of a specific material
questions.explanation: Design registration protects only the visual/aesthetic aspects. The functional elements (ergonomic support) are not covered by design law and would need a patent instead. Many products have both aesthetic and functional elements — they may need both design registration and patent protection.
questions.verify: Section 2(d) of the Designs Act, 2000 — design does not include any mode or principle of construction.

questions.prompt: Why is design registration particularly important for India's handicraft and textile industries?
options: These industries rely on unique visual patterns and shapes that can be easily copied; design registration helps artisans protect their creative work
Design registration is free for artisans
Artisans cannot apply for any other type of IP
Handicrafts are automatically registered
questions.explanation: India's handicraft and textile industries (silk sarees, block printing, pottery, metalwork) create highly visual and artistic products. Design registration is crucial because these patterns and shapes can be easily photographed and copied. Registration gives artisans legal power to stop copycats and protect their livelihood.
questions.verify: The Designs Act, 2000 is widely used in India's textile, handicraft, and consumer goods sectors. CIPAM and the Handicrafts Board promote IP awareness among artisans.

questions.prompt: Match the IP type to the correct description: 'Protects new inventions and processes for 20 years.'
options: Patent
Trademark
Copyright
Design
questions.explanation: A patent protects new inventions and processes. In India, a patent is valid for 20 years from the date of filing.
questions.verify: Section 53, Patents Act, 1970.

questions.prompt: Ritu writes a poem, Aman designs a logo for his shop, Kiran invents a new machine, and Deepa creates a unique bottle shape. Who should apply for a design registration?
options: Deepa — a unique bottle shape is a design
Ritu — a poem is a design
Aman — a logo is a design
Kiran — a machine is a design
questions.explanation: Deepa's unique bottle shape is a visual feature applied to a product — this is what design registration protects. Ritu's poem = copyright, Aman's logo = trademark, Kiran's machine = patent.
questions.verify: Each IP type protects a different kind of creation.

questions.prompt: Copyright protection in India requires the creator to register the work with the Copyright Office.
questions.explanation: False! Copyright is automatic in India. You get it the moment you create an original work. Registration is optional but helpful as proof of ownership.
questions.verify: Section 45, Copyright Act, 1957 — voluntary registration.

questions.prompt: A registered trademark in India can be renewed for how many years at a time?
options: 10 years
20 years
5 years
1 year
questions.explanation: A registered trademark can be renewed every 10 years, indefinitely, as long as the owner pays the renewal fee and continues using the mark.
questions.verify: Section 25, Trade Marks Act, 1999.

questions.prompt: Which of these is NOT a type of Intellectual Property?
options: Real estate (land and buildings)
Patents
Trademarks
Copyrights
questions.explanation: Real estate (land and buildings) is physical property, not intellectual property. IP includes patents, trademarks, copyrights, and designs — creations of the mind.
questions.verify: Intellectual property refers to creations of the mind — WIPO definition.

questions.prompt: A toy manufacturer copies the exact shape of another company's registered toy car. The internal mechanism is different. Which IP right is violated?
options: Design — the visual shape was copied
Patent — the toy was reverse-engineered
Trademark — the company name was copied
Copyright — the toy is an artistic work
questions.explanation: Design registration protects the visual appearance (shape). Even though the internal mechanism is different, copying the registered shape is design infringement.
questions.verify: Section 22, Designs Act, 2000.

questions.prompt: The ® symbol can be used for any trademark, even if it is not registered.
questions.explanation: False! The ® symbol can ONLY be used for trademarks that are officially registered. Using it falsely is a punishable offence. Unregistered marks should use ™ instead.
questions.verify: Section 107, Trade Marks Act, 1999 — penalty for falsely representing a mark as registered.

questions.prompt: Which Indian law governs patents?
options: The Patents Act, 1970
The Trade Marks Act, 1999
The Copyright Act, 1957
The Designs Act, 2000
questions.explanation: Patents in India are governed by the Patents Act, 1970, which has been amended several times (most notably in 2005 to include product patents).
questions.verify: The Patents Act, 1970 (as amended).

questions.prompt: A singer records a new song. How long is the copyright on the sound recording valid in India?
options: 60 years from publication
The singer's lifetime plus 60 years
20 years from recording
10 years from first performance
questions.explanation: Copyright in a sound recording lasts for 60 years from the beginning of the calendar year following publication. (Note: the underlying musical composition has a different term — the composer's lifetime plus 60 years.)
questions.verify: Section 26, Copyright Act, 1957.

questions.prompt: CIPAM stands for:
options: Cell for IPR Promotion and Management
Central Institute for Patent and Manufacturing
Copyright and Industrial Property Authority of Maharashtra
Controller of Industrial Patents and Marks
questions.explanation: CIPAM — Cell for IPR Promotion and Management — is an organisation under the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce and Industry, India. It promotes IP awareness across the country, including in schools!
questions.verify: CIPAM was established under the National IPR Policy, 2016 by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, Government of India.
